category: Core vocabulary: hygiene and the bathroom

entries.meaning: Soft paper on a roll, used in the bathroom after using the toilet. ---
examples: We're almost out of toilet paper.
Grab another roll of toilet paper from under the sink.
The stall had no toilet paper left.

entries.meaning: The hinged ring on top of a toilet that you sit on. ---
examples: Please put the toilet seat down when you're done.
The toilet seat is cracked and needs replacing.
Some public toilet seats have paper covers.

entries.meaning: A large towel for drying your body after a bath or shower. ---
examples: Hang your bath towel up so it dries.
The hotel left two fresh bath towels on the bed.
I wrapped myself in a bath towel and ran down the hall.

entries.meaning: A small towel kept by the sink for drying your hands. ---
examples: There's a clean hand towel by the sink.
She folded the hand towels into neat squares.
Use the hand towel, not the bath one.

entries.meaning: A sheet of thick absorbent paper used once for wiping or drying. ---
examples: Wipe that up with a paper towel.
We go through a roll of paper towels a week.
The restroom was out of paper towels.
entries.contrast: Americans say paper towels; the British call the kitchen kind kitchen roll.

entries.meaning: A plastic or fabric sheet that keeps water inside the shower. ---
examples: Pull the shower curtain closed or the floor gets soaked.
Our shower curtain has mildew along the bottom.
They sell shower curtains in every color.

entries.meaning: The fitting that sprays water down on you in the shower. ---
examples: The showerhead is clogged with mineral buildup.
He installed a new showerhead on Saturday.
Some showerheads come with a handheld hose.

entries.meaning: A small cupboard behind the bathroom mirror for pills and toiletries. ---
examples: The aspirin is in the medicine cabinet.
She keeps her contact lenses in the medicine cabinet.
Both medicine cabinets were stuffed with old prescriptions.
entries.contrast: In American English medicine has three syllables, MED-uh-suhn; British speakers usually say MED-sin.

entries.meaning: A wash in which you sit in a tub full of water. ---
examples: I took a long bath after work.
Give the baby a bath before bed.
Hot baths help my back.
entries.contrast: The plural baths is normally pronounced BATHZ with a voiced th; the British also say BAHTH for the singular.

entries.meaning: A small mat you step onto when getting out of the tub or shower. ---
examples: Step on the bath mat so you don't slip.
The bath mat was soaking wet.
We bought two matching bath mats.

entries.meaning: A bar or frame on the wall for hanging towels. ---
examples: Hang it on the towel rack.
The towel rack pulled right out of the drywall.
There are towel racks on both sides of the sink.
entries.contrast: Americans say towel rack; the British usually say towel rail.

entries.meaning: The round lower part of a toilet that holds water. ---
examples: Something is stuck in the toilet bowl.
Pour the cleaner around the rim of the toilet bowl.
The toilet bowls in that restroom were spotless.

entries.meaning: A long-handled brush for scrubbing the inside of a toilet. ---
examples: The toilet brush sits in a holder behind the tank.
Use the toilet brush, not a sponge.
We replaced both toilet brushes last month.

entries.meaning: The box behind a toilet that holds the water for flushing. ---
examples: The toilet tank keeps running after you flush.
He lifted the lid off the toilet tank to look inside.
Old toilet tanks use a lot more water.
entries.contrast: Americans say toilet tank; the British call it a cistern.

entries.meaning: A small enclosed space with a shower but no tub. ---
examples: The apartment has a shower stall instead of a tub.
Mold was growing in the corner of the shower stall.
Both shower stalls at the gym were taken.
entries.contrast: Americans say shower stall; the British say shower cubicle.

entries.meaning: A glass or plastic door that closes off a shower. ---
examples: The shower door won't slide anymore.
Wipe the shower door down after you use it.
Glass shower doors show every water spot.

entries.meaning: A rack or basket that hangs in the shower to hold soap and shampoo. ---
examples: Her shampoo is in the shower caddy.
Every dorm room needs a shower caddy.
The shower caddies hook right over the showerhead.

entries.meaning: A plastic cap worn to keep your hair dry in the shower. ---
examples: She wears a shower cap so she doesn't have to blow-dry.
The hotel left a shower cap by the sink.
The shower caps come free with the room.

entries.meaning: A device you stand on to see how much you weigh. ---
examples: The bathroom scale says I gained two pounds.
He steps on the bathroom scale every morning.
Digital bathroom scales are pretty cheap now.
entries.contrast: Americans weigh themselves on a scale; the British say scales, always plural.

entries.meaning: A machine in a public restroom that blows warm air to dry your hands. ---
examples: The hand dryer in that restroom is deafening.
There were no paper towels, just a hand dryer.
New hand dryers work in about ten seconds.

entries.meaning: A small dish that holds a bar of soap. ---
examples: Put the bar back in the soap dish.
The soap dish is full of slime.
Ceramic soap dishes crack if you drop them.

entries.meaning: A container that pumps out liquid soap. ---
examples: The soap dispenser is empty again.
Push the top of the soap dispenser twice.
They installed automatic soap dispensers in every restroom.

entries.meaning: A tool with a rubber blade for wiping water off glass or tile. ---
examples: Use the squeegee on the shower door.
He keeps a squeegee hanging inside the shower.
The gas station had squeegees by every pump.

entries.meaning: The hard paste that fills the lines between tiles. ---
examples: The grout between the tiles is turning black.
We had the grout cleaned and resealed.
Bleach whitens grout pretty fast.

entries.meaning: A bar mounted on a wall to hold on to in a tub or shower. ---
examples: We put a grab bar in my mother's shower.
Hold the grab bar when you step out.
Hotel bathrooms usually have grab bars by the toilet.

entries.meaning: A fan that pulls steam and smells out of a bathroom. ---
examples: Turn on the exhaust fan before you shower.
The exhaust fan rattles the whole time it runs.
Bathrooms without windows need exhaust fans.
entries.contrast: The h in exhaust is silent: ig-ZAWST.

entries.meaning: A wall fixture in a men's restroom for urinating into. ---
examples: The urinal on the end is out of order.
He waited while someone finished at the urinal.
All three urinals had been replaced.
entries.contrast: Americans stress the first syllable, YUR-uh-nuhl; the British say yoo-RY-nuhl.

entries.meaning: A low bathroom fixture for washing yourself after using the toilet. ---
examples: The hotel bathroom had a bidet.
Americans rarely grow up with a bidet in the house.
Bidets are common in France and Japan.
entries.contrast: The final t is silent, and Americans stress the second syllable: bih-DAY.

entries.meaning: A room or fixture for washing and using the toilet, especially on a plane. ---
examples: The lavatory at the back of the plane is occupied.
Please return to your seat when the lavatory is free.
The lavatories were cleaned between flights.

entries.meaning: A public room with toilets and sinks. ---
examples: The washroom is down the hall on your left.
He asked the waiter where the washroom was.
Both washrooms were being mopped.
entries.contrast: Most Americans say restroom or bathroom; washroom is the usual word in Canada.

entries.meaning: A small wooden toilet building standing outside, with no plumbing. ---
examples: The cabin has an outhouse out back.
Nobody wants to use an outhouse in January.
The old farm still had two outhouses.

entries.meaning: A small toilet or bowl that a young child learns to use. ---
examples: He sat on the potty for ten minutes.
She asked to use the potty.
We keep two potties in the house.

entries.meaning: A portable plastic toilet set up at outdoor events and building sites. ---
examples: There's a porta-potty by the parking lot.
The line for the porta-potty was twenty people deep.
They trucked in a dozen porta-potties for the race.

entries.meaning: The process of teaching a young child to use the toilet. ---
examples: We started potty training this summer.
Potty training took about three weeks.
Her pediatrician had advice about potty training.

entries.meaning: A simple toilet, often just a pit, used at a camp or army base. ---
examples: The soldiers dug a latrine behind the tents.
Camp rules said to keep the latrine clean.
The latrines were downhill from the water supply.

entries.meaning: The water in a bathtub. ---
examples: The bathwater is getting cold.
She tested the bathwater with her elbow.
Don't throw the baby out with the bathwater.

entries.meaning: Soap made for washing your hands, usually liquid. ---
examples: We're out of hand soap.
The hand soap in the kitchen smells like lemon.
Refill the hand soap by the sink.

entries.meaning: Liquid soap for washing your body in the shower. ---
examples: He switched from bar soap to body wash.
The body wash smells like coconut.
Buy the body wash that's on sale.

entries.meaning: A thick liquid soap used in the shower. ---
examples: The hotel gives you tiny bottles of shower gel.
I like shower gel better than a bar of soap.
She squeezed some shower gel onto a loofah.

entries.meaning: An alcohol gel that kills germs on your hands without water. ---
examples: There's hand sanitizer by the door.
She keeps hand sanitizer in her purse.
The office ran out of hand sanitizer.

entries.meaning: A shaver with moving blades that runs on a motor. ---
examples: He shaves with an electric razor.
My electric razor needs charging.
Electric razors are quicker but not as close.

entries.meaning: A cheap plastic razor that is thrown away after a few uses. ---
examples: He bought a pack of disposable razors.
A disposable razor is fine for one trip.
Disposable razors go dull fast.

entries.meaning: A handheld machine that blows hot air to dry hair. ---
examples: Can I borrow your hair dryer?
The hair dryer blew a fuse.
Most hotel rooms have hair dryers on the wall.
entries.contrast: Americans call the same thing a hair dryer or a blow dryer.

entries.meaning: A small stiff brush for cleaning under and around the nails. ---
examples: Scrub your hands with the nail brush.
There's a nail brush by the garage sink.
Mechanics keep nail brushes handy.

entries.meaning: A product put under the arms to stop you from sweating. ---
examples: This antiperspirant actually works.
He put on antiperspirant before the interview.
Most antiperspirants cover the smell too.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: Fine white powder patted on skin to keep it dry. ---
examples: She sprinkled baby powder on the changing table.
Baby powder keeps the rash from coming back.
The whole bathroom smelled like baby powder.

entries.meaning: A soft mineral powder used on the skin to absorb moisture. ---
examples: He dusted his feet with talcum powder.
Talcum powder keeps your shoes from smelling.
A little talcum powder stops the chafing.

entries.meaning: A small moist cloth sold in a pack for cleaning skin or surfaces. ---
examples: Hand me a wipe for the baby's face.
She cleaned the counter with a disinfecting wipe.
We buy wipes by the case.

entries.meaning: A rough sponge used to scrub the skin in the shower. ---
examples: She scrubbed her back with a loofah.
Replace the loofah every month or so.
The loofahs hang on a hook in the shower.

entries.meaning: A light rough stone used to rub hard skin off the feet. ---
examples: Use a pumice stone on your heels.
The pumice stone sits on the edge of the tub.
Pumice stones float, since the rock is full of air.
entries.contrast: Pumice is PUM-uhs, with the vowel of cup, not POO-mis.

entries.meaning: Soap that foams up in the tub, or a bath taken with it. ---
examples: The kids want a bubble bath tonight.
She poured bubble bath under the running water.
Long bubble baths are her way of relaxing.
entries.русский: пена для ванны; ванна с пеной
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: Scented crystals dissolved in bathwater to soften it. ---
examples: She dumped bath salts into the tub.
These bath salts smell like eucalyptus.
A jar of bath salts makes an easy gift.
entries.contrast: Always plural in form: bath salts, never a bath salt.

entries.meaning: A hard ball of scented powder that fizzes in bathwater. ---
examples: Drop the bath bomb in and watch it fizz.
She got a set of bath bombs for her birthday.
That bath bomb turned the water bright blue.
entries.contrast: The b at the end of bomb is silent: BAHM.

entries.meaning: Scented oil added to bathwater to soften the skin. ---
examples: A few drops of bath oil is plenty.
The bath oil left a ring around the tub.
She uses bath oil when her skin is dry.

entries.meaning: A spray or holder that puts a pleasant smell into a room. ---
examples: Spray some air freshener in the bathroom.
The air freshener smells like fake pine.
They plug air fresheners into every outlet.

entries.meaning: A thick clear grease spread on dry skin or small cuts. ---
examples: Put a little petroleum jelly on the scrape.
Petroleum jelly keeps her lips from cracking.
A jar of petroleum jelly lasts for years.

entries.meaning: A light scented spray put on the body. ---
examples: The locker room reeked of body spray.
He got three body sprays for Christmas.
She wears body spray instead of perfume.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: Soap sold in solid pieces rather than as a liquid. ---
examples: I still prefer bar soap.
Bar soap lasts longer than body wash.
The hotel leaves a small piece of bar soap by the sink.

entries.meaning: A wash done with a wet cloth instead of getting into a tub. ---
examples: The nurse gave him a sponge bath.
With the cast on, he was stuck taking sponge baths.
A sponge bath is better than nothing.

entries.meaning: A small plug of cotton used inside the body during a period. ---
examples: She keeps tampons in her bag.
The dispenser in the restroom sells tampons for a quarter.
He was sent to the store for a box of tampons.

entries.meaning: An absorbent pad worn in underwear during a period. ---
examples: The machine in the restroom sells sanitary pads.
She put a sanitary pad in her purse.
Sanitary pads come in different thicknesses.
entries.contrast: Americans say sanitary pad or just pad; the British say sanitary towel.

entries.meaning: A chemical that kills germs on surfaces. ---
examples: Wipe the counter with disinfectant.
The whole clinic smelled of disinfectant.
Some disinfectants have to sit for a full minute.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A liquid put on skin or a wound to stop infection. ---
examples: She dabbed antiseptic on the cut.
The antiseptic stung for a second.
Most first aid kits include an antiseptic.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A clear alcohol used to clean skin, cuts, and surfaces. ---
examples: Clean the thermometer with rubbing alcohol.
A bottle of rubbing alcohol costs about a dollar.
Rubbing alcohol evaporates in seconds.
entries.contrast: American rubbing alcohol is called surgical spirit in Britain.

entries.meaning: A clear liquid that bubbles on a wound and kills germs. ---
examples: Pour a little hydrogen peroxide on it.
Hydrogen peroxide foams the moment it touches a cut.
The brown bottle of hydrogen peroxide is in the cabinet.

entries.meaning: A strong chemical poured into a pipe to dissolve a blockage. ---
examples: Pour drain cleaner down the sink and wait.
Drain cleaner can burn your skin.
None of the drain cleaners touched that clog.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A stiff brush for scrubbing floors, tile, and tubs. ---
examples: Take a scrub brush to the tile.
The scrub brush is under the sink.
We wore out two scrub brushes on that bathroom.
entries.contrast: Americans say scrub brush; the British say scrubbing brush.

entries.meaning: A rough pad used to scrub off stuck-on dirt. ---
examples: She went after the tub with a scouring pad.
A scouring pad will scratch that finish.
The box holds six scouring pads.

entries.meaning: Waterproof gloves worn to protect your hands while cleaning. ---
examples: Put on rubber gloves before you use the bleach.
The rubber gloves are under the sink.
She peeled off her yellow rubber gloves.
entries.contrast: Normally plural: a pair of rubber gloves.

entries.meaning: The products and tools kept in a house for cleaning. ---
examples: The cleaning supplies are under the sink.
Keep cleaning supplies away from small children.
The roommates split the cost of cleaning supplies.
entries.contrast: Nearly always plural in this sense.

entries.meaning: Soap made for washing clothes in a machine. ---
examples: We're almost out of laundry detergent.
Use half a cap of laundry detergent.
That laundry detergent smells too strong.

entries.meaning: A liquid added in the wash to make clothes feel soft. ---
examples: Add fabric softener to the last rinse.
Fabric softener makes towels less absorbent.
She skips the fabric softener for the baby's clothes.
entries.contrast: The t in softener is silent: SAWF-nur.

entries.meaning: A scented sheet tossed in the dryer to stop static. ---
examples: Throw a dryer sheet in with the towels.
The box of dryer sheets is on the shelf.
One dryer sheet is enough for a small load.

entries.meaning: A product sprayed on a mark to lift it out of fabric. ---
examples: Spray stain remover on it before you wash it.
The stain remover took the coffee right out.
None of the stain removers worked on the ink.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: The state of being clean, or the habit of keeping things clean. ---
examples: The restaurant was cited for poor cleanliness.
She's fussy about cleanliness in the kitchen.
Cleanliness matters more than fancy fixtures.
entries.contrast: Pronounced KLEN-lee-nuhs, with the vowel of pen, though clean has the vowel of see.

entries.meaning: Systems for keeping people healthy by removing waste and dirt. ---
examples: Poor sanitation spreads disease.
The city's sanitation department picks up on Tuesdays.
Clean water and sanitation have saved millions of lives.

entries.meaning: Waste water and human waste carried away in pipes. ---
examples: Raw sewage leaked into the creek.
The plant treats sewage from four towns.
There was a smell of sewage in the basement.
entries.contrast: Sewage is the waste itself; the pipe that carries it away is a sewer.

entries.meaning: An underground tank that holds household waste where there are no sewers. ---
examples: The house is on a septic tank, not city sewer.
A septic tank has to be pumped every few years.
Country properties usually have septic tanks.

entries.meaning: A covered pit that collects waste water and sewage. ---
examples: The old farmhouse still had a cesspool.
The cesspool overflowed after the storm.
Health inspectors ordered the cesspools filled in.

entries.meaning: The presence of germs or dirt where they do not belong. ---
examples: The lab found contamination in the water supply.
Washing your hands prevents contamination.
They shut the plant down after the contamination.

entries.meaning: Disgusting dirt. ---
examples: The kitchen was covered in filth.
He scrubbed years of filth off the tile.
You could smell the filth from the hallway.

entries.meaning: Dirt that has built up and stuck to a surface. ---
examples: The window was black with grime.
It took a scrub brush to get the grime off.
Hot water and soap cut through the grime.

entries.meaning: The dull film that soap leaves on tubs and shower doors. ---
examples: Soap scum built up on the glass door.
Vinegar takes off soap scum.
There's a ring of soap scum around the tub.

entries.meaning: Soapy bubbles on the surface of water. ---
examples: The sink was full of suds.
Suds spilled over the edge of the tub.
Rinse until there are no suds left.
entries.contrast: Always plural in form and takes a plural verb: the suds were everywhere.

entries.meaning: Waste material that is thrown away. ---
examples: The city collects household refuse on Mondays.
Piles of refuse sat outside the building.
The sign forbids dumping refuse here.
entries.contrast: The noun is REF-yooss; the verb refuse, meaning to say no, is rih-FYOOZ.

entries.meaning: A smell, usually an unpleasant one. ---
examples: There's a strange odor coming from the drain.
The odor of bleach filled the room.
Odors build up in a bathroom with no fan.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it odor; the British spell it odour.

entries.meaning: A very strong, disgusting smell. ---
examples: The stench from the garbage was unbearable.
A stench hit us the moment we opened the door.
Nothing covers the stench of a backed-up sewer.

entries.meaning: The work of making a dirty place clean again. ---
examples: The cleanup took all afternoon.
Whoever makes the mess handles the cleanup.
The party was fun; the cleanups never are.

entries.meaning: The act of washing your hands to remove germs. ---
examples: Handwashing is the simplest way to stop germs.
Signs in the restroom remind employees about handwashing.
Careful handwashing takes a full twenty seconds.

entries.meaning: A long stay in hot water, or a period of leaving something in liquid. ---
examples: She treated herself to a long soak in the tub.
Give the towel a soak in cold water.
Hot soaks help sore muscles.

entries.meaning: The care you take of your hair, nails, and general appearance. ---
examples: The job listing mentioned neat grooming.
Grooming takes him about ten minutes in the morning.
Personal grooming products are in aisle four.

entries.meaning: Keeping your own body clean and healthy. ---
examples: Good personal hygiene prevents a lot of illness.
The class covers personal hygiene and nutrition.
His personal hygiene had slipped while he was sick.

entries.meaning: Care of the teeth and gums by brushing and flossing. ---
examples: The dentist praised her oral hygiene.
Oral hygiene means more than just brushing.
Poor oral hygiene leads to gum disease.

entries.meaning: Thin string pulled between the teeth to clean them. ---
examples: A piece of dental floss got stuck between my teeth.
Buy the waxed dental floss.
Dental floss reaches where a brush cannot.

entries.meaning: The soft sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth. ---
examples: Brushing removes plaque before it hardens.
The hygienist scraped the plaque off.
Plaque builds up along the gum line.
entries.contrast: Spelled with a silent -que and pronounced PLAK.

entries.meaning: Hardened plaque that only a dentist can scrape off. ---
examples: Tartar had built up behind his front teeth.
This toothpaste claims to fight tartar.
Only a professional cleaning removes tartar.

entries.meaning: The hard white outer layer of a tooth. ---
examples: Soda wears away tooth enamel.
Once enamel is gone, it doesn't grow back.
The dentist said my enamel is thin.

entries.meaning: An unpleasant smell coming from someone's mouth. ---
examples: Coffee gives him bad breath.
Mouthwash only hides bad breath.
Bad breath can be a sign of gum trouble.

entries.meaning: A plastic and wire device worn to keep teeth straight after braces. ---
examples: Wear your retainer every night.
He lost his retainer in the cafeteria.
Retainers cost a few hundred dollars to replace.

entries.meaning: A removable set of false teeth. ---
examples: Grandpa soaks his dentures overnight.
Her dentures fit better after the adjustment.
He got dentures at seventy.
entries.contrast: Normally plural: a set of dentures, not a denture.

entries.meaning: Treatment that makes teeth look whiter. ---
examples: She paid for professional whitening.
Whitening can make your teeth sensitive.
The strips promise whitening in two weeks.

entries.meaning: Infection of the gums that can loosen the teeth. ---
examples: Flossing helps prevent gum disease.
Gum disease is more common than people think.
He's being treated for early gum disease.

entries.meaning: The slow breaking down of a tooth that produces cavities. ---
examples: Sugar is the main cause of tooth decay.
Fluoride slows tooth decay.
The X-ray showed tooth decay between two molars.

entries.meaning: A pain in a tooth. ---
examples: I've had a toothache since Sunday.
A bad toothache kept him up all night.
Toothaches rarely go away on their own.
entries.contrast: The -ache ending is pronounced AYK, as in cake.

entries.meaning: One of the four back teeth that come in during your late teens or twenties. ---
examples: My wisdom tooth is coming in sideways.
She had all four wisdom teeth pulled.
Not everyone gets wisdom teeth.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: one wisdom tooth, two wisdom teeth.

entries.meaning: One of the first small teeth that a child loses around age six. ---
examples: He lost his first baby tooth today.
All her baby teeth are gone now.
A baby tooth usually falls out on its own.
entries.contrast: Americans say baby tooth; the British often say milk tooth. The plural is baby teeth.

entries.meaning: Dental treatment that cleans out the inside of a damaged tooth. ---
examples: He needs a root canal on his back molar.
The root canal took two visits.
Root canals aren't as painful as people say.

entries.meaning: A dentist who straightens crooked teeth with braces. ---
examples: The orthodontist tightened her braces.
We see the orthodontist every six weeks.
Most orthodontists start treatment around age twelve.

entries.meaning: One of the flat front teeth used for biting. ---
examples: He chipped an incisor on a fork.
Your top incisors do most of the biting.
The dentist filled a small cavity in an incisor.

entries.meaning: The unpleasant smell of stale sweat. ---
examples: Deodorant keeps body odor under control.
The gym reeked of body odor.
Nobody wants to be told they have body odor.

entries.meaning: Sweat, or the process of sweating. ---
examples: Perspiration ran down his forehead.
The shirt was soaked with perspiration.
Perspiration is how the body cools itself.
entries.contrast: Perspiration is the polite word; in ordinary speech Americans say sweat.

entries.meaning: The egg of a head louse, stuck to a hair. ---
examples: The school nurse checked the kids for nits.
Every nit has to be combed out.
Nits look like tiny white specks.

entries.meaning: A hair that curls back and grows into the skin. ---
examples: He gets ingrown hairs after shaving.
An ingrown hair can look like a pimple.
Exfoliating helps with ingrown hairs.

entries.meaning: A patch of thick hard skin, usually on a hand or foot. ---
examples: He has calluses from playing guitar.
A pumice stone smooths a callus down.
Her heels were covered in calluses.
entries.contrast: The noun is callus; callous, spelled with an o, is the adjective meaning unfeeling.

entries.meaning: The soft yellow substance that forms inside the ear. ---
examples: Earwax actually protects the ear canal.
The doctor flushed out a plug of earwax.
Cotton swabs push earwax in deeper.

entries.meaning: An itchy fungal infection of the skin between the toes.
examples: He picked up athlete's foot at the pool.
Athlete's foot spreads in damp locker rooms.
The cream cleared up his athlete's foot in a week.
